summary: This document defines a way to convey vendor-specific constraints and objective functions in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol. Path computation requests carry details of constraints, and this adds a standard way to carry custom ones. It was replaced by RFC 7470.

plainLanguage.summary: Route planners usually ask for fastest or shortest. This lets a company add its own special wishes in a standard way. It has been replaced by RFC 7470.

questions: how do vendors add custom constraints to pcep
what is an enterprise number in pcep
how does pcep handle vendor extensions
subtitle: Adding vendor-specific extensions to path computation protocol requests

tldr.problem: Path Computation Elements (PCEs) need to support vendor-specific constraints and objective functions beyond the standardized options, but PCEP had no standard way to include proprietary information.
tldr.mechanism: Defines two new PCEP constructs: the VENDOR-INFORMATION object for standalone vendor data, and the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV (Type-Length-Variable) that can be embedded in existing PCEP objects. Both use an Enterprise Number to identify the vendor.
tldr.outcome: Vendors can now extend PCEP with proprietary constraints without breaking interoperability. The mechanism was later updated by RFC 7470.

today: RFC 7150 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 7470, which extended the mechanism for managing relationships between multiple path computations. However, the core vendor information mechanism from RFC 7150 remains in use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a network component that computes paths or routes based on network constraints. PCEP is the protocol that clients and PCEs use to exchange path computation requests and responses.

PCEP already allows clients to specify constraints like bandwidth requirements and maximum hop counts, as well as objective functions that define what makes a path "good" (for example, minimum cost or minimum delay). However, vendors sometimes need to support proprietary constraints and objective functions specific to their equipment. PCEP's objective function registry has space for vendor-specific codes, but there was no way to send the detailed vendor-specific information itself. This document solves that problem by defining a standard mechanism for carrying vendor extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a delivery company has special rules like "avoid certain roads" or "prefer routes through our own hubs". This RFC explains how to tell the route planner about those custom rules.

sections.title: The Vendor Information Constructs
sections.content:
RFC 7150 defines two new protocol elements, both of which use an Enterprise Number (a globally unique 32-bit identifier assigned by IANA) to indicate which vendor's proprietary format is being used.

The VENDOR-INFORMATION object is a standalone PCEP object that carries vendor-specific data. It can appear in path computation request (PCReq) and response (PCRep) messages. A P flag in the object header controls whether the receiving PCE must understand it (if set) or can safely ignore it (if not set).

The VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV (Type-Length-Variable) is a more flexible mechanism that can be embedded inside any PCEP object that supports TLVs. This allows vendors to attach proprietary information to specific protocol elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like two ways to send a note: a standalone letter (the object) or a note attached to an existing letter (the TLV). Both include a company ID so everyone knows whose rules are inside.

sections.title: Format and Protocol Rules
sections.content:
Both the VENDOR-INFORMATION object and TLV have the same simple format. The first field is a 32-bit Enterprise Number that identifies the vendor. The rest of the space is left entirely to the vendor to define; it contains whatever proprietary information the vendor needs to send.

A PCE that receives vendor information uses the Enterprise Number to determine whether it understands that vendor's format. If a PCE does not recognize the Enterprise Number, it follows the P flag: if P is set, the PCE must reject the message; if P is not set, the PCE can safely ignore the vendor-specific data and continue processing the rest of the request.

Multiple instances of vendor information from different vendors can appear in a single message, each with its own Enterprise Number.
sections.plainLanguage: Each vendor's data starts with a company ID number. If a PCE sees an ID it doesn't recognize, the P flag tells it whether the whole request is ruined or if it can skip that company's special rules.

sections.title: How Vendor Information Flows
sections.content:
A Path Computation Client (PCC) that wants to use vendor-specific constraints includes the VENDOR-INFORMATION object or TLV in its PCReq message. The PCE examines the Enterprise Number inside. If the PCE is from that vendor (or has been configured to understand that vendor's format), it processes the vendor-specific data along with the standard constraints. If not, it consults the P flag to decide whether to reject or ignore the data.

Vendor-specific information can be included at several places in a PCReq: in the synchronized path computation list (for coordinated multi-request computations) or within individual path computation requests. The RFC's encoding rules follow the existing PCEP message syntax.

A PCE can also include vendor information in its response (PCRep message) to communicate vendor-specific results or status back to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: A client adds a note saying "I want you to use this company's special rules." The route planner reads the company ID and either applies the rules (if it knows them) or throws away the note and keeps going (if the rules are optional).

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
PCE implementations that do not support RFC 7150 will not recognize the VENDOR-INFORMATION object or TLV. According to PCEP's standard rules for unknown objects and TLVs, an older implementation treats them as unrecognized and follows the P flag. If P is set, it rejects the entire message with an "Unknown Object" error. If P is not set, it silently ignores the vendor data and processes the rest of the message. This allows older and newer systems to interoperate gracefully.

Vendors are encouraged to document their proprietary extensions and, when there is broad interest, to bring successful extensions to the IETF for standardization as regular PCEP features.
sections.plainLanguage: Old route planners don't understand the new company rules, but they know to either reject the request (if it says the rules are required) or to skip them (if they're optional). That way old and new systems don't break each other.
